lawyer:
A.F.M.A. Rahman with Ahsanullah Khan ------ For Petitioners.
Abu Salek ------ for Opposite party.
parties:
Md. Nurul Hoque Khan & ors ------ Petitioners.
Vs.
Manager Bangladesh Bank ------ Opposite party.
full_judgment:
This Rule at the instance of the plaintiffs is directed against the judgment and order passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 4th Court, Dhaka in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 506 of 1984 reversing the judgment and order of the learned Munsif, 6th Court, Dhaka allowing an application for temporary injunction under Order 39, Rule 1 C.P.C. in Title Suit No. 310 of 1984 for declaration. 

 2. The plaintiffs instituted the suit for declaration that the allotment of accommodation under order No. 37/84 issued by the defendant, Bangladesh Bank in pursuance of the recommendation of the Allotment of Accommodation Committee, to the employees of Bangladesh Bank is illegal, void and inoperative alleging that the plaintiffs are 'B' category staff holding different posts of Assistant Treasurers in Dhaka station of the Bangladesh Bank, and that in terms of the Rules for 'Allotment of Accommodation' of the employee of Bangladesh Bank allotments are required to be made strictly on the basis of a joint seniority of the employees of 'B' and 'C' categories in Dhaka in respect of 'Kha' type flat at Motijheel and R.K. Mission Road and 'C' type flat at IG Bagan and that on the basis of an illegal recommendation of Allotment of the 'Accommodation Committee' and in violation of the aforesaid Allotment Rules 137 flats of the Bank under the aforesaid office order has been illegally allotted to several 'B' and 'C' Category staff of the Bank. It has been alleged that several employees who have got allotment of accommodation in pursuance of the said impugned order No. 37/84 are juniors to the plaintiffs in service as well as in the station and as such many of them were not entitled to the accommodation allotted to them and those have been done in clear violation of the Rules. 

 3. Upon filing of the suit the plaintiffs filed an application for temporary injunction to restrain the Bangladesh Bank from not giving effect to the impugned order of allotment. The Bangladesh Bank filed an objection against the application for temporary injunction. The Bank has alleged that the plaintiff belonged to 'A' category staff and that B category staff are entitled to get 'Kha' type flat at Motijheel and R.K. Mission Road and 'C' type flat at I.G. Bagan along with the Category staffs. 

 5. The learned Munsif upon hearing the objection against the application for temporary injunction allowed the application and restrained the Bank from giving effect to the impugned order of allotment. On appeal the learned Subordinate Judge reversed the decision of the learned Munsif and rejected the application for temporary injunction. Hence this Rule under section 115, CPC at the instance of the plaintiffs. 

 6. Mr. A.F.M.A. Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-petitioners has submitted that the court of appeal below having has gone into the merit of the case of the plaintiffs and upon deciding the same he has rejected the application for temporary injunction and as such he has committed an error of law resulting in an error of decision in reversing the judgment of the learned Munsif in as much as that the court is to see whether the plaintiffs have a prima facie case and entitled to an order of injunction to restrain the defendant  from giving effect to the impugned order of allotment. In this connection the learned Advocate has referred to the decision reported in 28 D.L.R. (S.C.) 415. It is an accepted proposition of law that for grant of a relief by way of temporary injunction under Order 39, Rule 1, C.P.C. the court need not enter into the merit of the case as is necessary for passing a decree after hearing the evidence of the parties. If the plaintiff has a prima facie and arguable case he would be entitled to an order of injunction pending disposal of the suit so that the subject matter of the suit may not be washed or destroyed. It appears from the judgment of the court of appeal below that it has considered the case of the parties and has gone into the Allotment Rules for determination as to whether the plaintiffs have prima facie case for an order of temporary injunction. In considering the case of the parties and the relevant Accommodation. Rules it cannot be said that the court upon deciding the merit of the case of the plaintiffs, as if in trial, has reversed the judgment of the trial court and refused to grant injunction. For a decision as to whether the plaintiffs would. be entitled to order of a temporary injunction it was necessary for the learned subordinate judge hearing the appeal to consider the facts of the case of the parties and the relevant Rules regarding allotment of accommodation to the employees of 'B' and 'C' categories of the Bank and satisfy himself as to the prima facie right of the plaintiffs. In that view of the matter I do not find any substance in the contention of the Learned Advocate for the plaintiffs that the court of appeal below has committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision in rejecting the application for temporary injunction. 

 7. The learned Advocate for the plaintiffs has next submitted that the Accommodation Rules have been approved by the Government but he could not show anything in support of his contention. The defendant has filed an affidavit-in-opposition stating that these Rules have not been approved under Article 82 of the Bangladesh Bank Order 1973. Since there in no affidavit in reply or anything has been produced by the plaintiffs to show that the rules have been approved by the Government, it appears to me that there is no force in the contention of the learned Advocate for the plaintiffs that the Rules have been approved by the Government under Articles 82 and it has the force of law as a regulation. 

 8. The learned Advocate for the plaintiffs has next submitted that the Accommodation Rules have been violated in marking the impugned allotments under Order 37/84 in as much as these allotments have been made on the basis of two waiting lists, one for 'B' category staff and the other for 'C' category staff which is not permissible under the Rules and that the allotments in pursuance thereof have been made illegally and in violation of Rule 6 of the Allotment of Accommodation Rules. Upon a perusal of Rule 4 of the aforesaid Rules it appears that 'B' and 'C' categories of staff are entitled to 'Kha' type flat at Motijheel and R.K. Mission Road and 'C' type flat at I.G. Bagan. These flats are meant for accommodation of these two categories of employees. A waiting list for each class of accommodation are to be prepared under Rule 6 of the aforesaid Accommodation Rules. Rule 6 contemplates that there should be one list for each class of accommodation for allotment to the staffs entitled to them, and the criteria for selection would be on the basis of seniority of joining in the station, i.e. one who is posted in the station earlier he will have preference for inclusion in the waiting list than the person who is posted in the station later. 

 11. Mr. A.F.M.A. Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff petitioners has submitted that even conceding that the allotment rules have not been approved under Article 82 of P.O. 127 of 1972 yet the Bangladesh Bank is bound by the Rules under which right to the employees have been given as regards their accommodation in the flats of the Bank. 

 In support of his contention he has referred to the decision reported in 29 D.L.R. (S.C.) 41. In that decision it appears that the regulation was framed by a statutory authority to whom powers were delegated by law to frame regulations. In that view the decision is of no assistance to the learned Advocate for the plaintiffs. Similarly the other decision, namely, P.L.D.1964(S.C.) 21 is of no in assistance to the plaintiffs since facts are quite distinguishable from the facts of the instant case. 

 12. It appears, as I have referred to above, two lists have been prepared for accommodation of one type of flats though it is not con template under Rule 6 of the Accommodation Rules. But however in the absence of any Regulation these Rules of the Bank's rule cannot be treated as binding statutory Rules and they should be considered as Rules for guidance giving no vested right to any employee affected by them. I am also of the view that preparation of two waiting lists for two categories of employees for the same type of accommodation was made by the Bank in the interest of justice and equity. In view of the above I therefore, do not find any illegality in the impugned order of accommodation. I also hold that these Rules having no force of law as it has not been approved by the Government under Article 82 of the Bangladesh Bank Order, 1972 the plaintiffs appear to have no prima facie case for an order of temporary injunction and the learned Subordinate Judge has rightly rejected the application for temporary injunction and allowed the appeal.
